analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling along the entire Atlantic Coast.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 13 coastal senators, was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in April 2015 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently bar the Interior Department from selling or approving any lease for oil, gas, or mineral drilling in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, and South Atlantic planning areas [S2][S3]. That covers federal waters off the entire East Coast. The stated aim is to protect Atlantic beaches, tourism, and fisheries from the risk of offshore spills. It never moved beyond its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, tourism businesses, and fishing industries along the Atlantic seaboard, which would be shielded from oil spills and drilling infrastructure. Beachgoers and residents of Atlantic coast states also gain the environmental protection the bill locks in permanently rather than leaving it to each administration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coast towns, beaches, and fisheries

how_it_helps.text: Permanently prohibits the Interior Department from issuing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, and South Atlantic planning areas [S2][S3].
Writes the ban directly into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, so it cannot be reversed by a future administration changing its own leasing plan [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to a new drilling frontier, and the federal government would forgo any royalties from Atlantic production. Energy consumers could face marginally higher supply risk, though East Coast production was prospective rather than established.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers seeking Atlantic leases

drawbacks.text: The ban removes a potential source of domestic oil and gas supply, which supporters of Atlantic drilling argued could add jobs and revenue for coastal states and royalties for the federal treasury.
A permanent statutory ban forecloses the option even if safety technology, local sentiment, or energy conditions change, which critics of drilling moratoria consider too rigid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tradeoff is a known, concentrated risk — an oil spill along developed Atlantic beaches and fisheries — against speculative gains from a drilling region that had no producing wells. The permanence is the bill's main selling point and its main criticism. Economically, the industries most exposed to a spill (tourism and fishing) are far larger employers in Atlantic coast states than drilling would have been, but the lost energy supply is a real cost that drilling supporters weigh heavily.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the COAST Anti-Drilling Act on April 22, 2015, with nine original cosponsors listed on the introduced bill [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on April 22, 2015 [S5].
The action history shows no further activity — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — after the committee referral [S5].
Twelve senators cosponsored the bill: 11 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies, which kept Atlantic offshore areas available for potential leasing, and senators from energy-producing states who never had to cast a recorded vote on it. Atlantic drilling remained a live policy question into the next administration.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies eyeing Atlantic leases

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban Atlantic offshore drilling and championed it as New Jersey's senator.

for.name: 12 Senate cosponsors (11 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Cosponsors, including Markey, Booker, Sanders, Mikulski, Cardin, Whitehouse, Warren, Blumenthal, and Reed
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from coastal or New England states.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill in the full two years of the 114th Congress [S5].

against.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled it for consideration; she is from Alaska, an oil-producing state whose industry strongly opposed new drilling bans.

against.name: 41 Senate Republicans plus energy-state Democrats
against.role: Enough senators to block floor action had it advanced
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no path to the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster even if it had cleared committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 supporters were Democrats or independents from Atlantic coast states; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Energy Committee and Senate never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently shut them out of the Atlantic outer continental shelf, eliminating a prospective frontier for exploration and production. Because drilling profits depend on access to waters that coastal communities use for tourism and fishing, the industry's interest runs against the coastal public's in this fight.

industries.industry: Atlantic coastal tourism and commercial fishing
industries.note: A permanent ban protects beaches, resort economies, and fisheries from the risk of spills and drilling infrastructure. These industries' fortunes rise and fall with clean water and beaches, the same thing the bill protects.
